common_defenses: Good faith belief — the defendant genuinely believed the report was accurate when filed.
Mistake — the inaccuracies in the report were honest errors, not intentional fabrications.
Retraction — the defendant corrected the report before any harm resulted.
The report was substantially true, with only minor inaccuracies.

prosecution_strengths: Text messages, voicemails, and social media posts provide documentary evidence of the threat.
Victim testimony about the fear caused by the threat is compelling.
Context evidence (prior conflicts, domestic violence history) supports the seriousness of the threat.
defense_opportunities: First Amendment — the statement was hyperbole, venting, or political speech, not a true threat.
The statement was conditional or hypothetical and did not place a reasonable person in fear.
Context shows the statement was made in jest and was not taken seriously by the recipient.
The defendant did not intend the statement to be threatening.
common_defenses: Not a 'true threat' — the statement was protected speech, hyperbole, or rhetorical.
No intent to threaten — the defendant did not mean the statement as a threat.
The alleged victim's fear was unreasonable given the context.
The statement was conditional and not an imminent threat of violence.

prosecution_strengths: Transcript evidence and prior sworn statements provide direct proof of the false testimony.
Contradictory evidence showing the truth of the matter establishes the falsity.
The 'material matter' element is broadly interpreted by courts.
defense_opportunities: The statement was literally true, even if misleading — perjury requires a false statement of fact.
The defendant genuinely believed the statement was true when made.
The statement was not 'material' to the proceeding — it concerned an insignificant detail.
Ambiguity in the question asked led to a misunderstanding, not intentional falsehood.
common_defenses: Good faith belief — the defendant believed the statement was true.
Literally true — the statement, while misleading, was technically accurate.
Immaterial — the false statement did not relate to a material issue.
Ambiguity — the question was unclear and the answer was reasonable given its phrasing.

prosecution_strengths: Financial records tracing payments between the defendant and the official provide direct evidence.
Electronic communications discussing the exchange are powerful proof.
Cooperating witnesses (often the official or an intermediary) provide testimony.
defense_opportunities: The payment was a lawful campaign contribution or gift within legal limits.
No quid pro quo — there was no agreement linking the payment to any official action.
The defendant did not know the recipient was a public official or that the payment was improper.
Entrapment — law enforcement solicited the bribe.
common_defenses: Lawful contribution — the payment was a legitimate campaign donation or gift.
No quid pro quo — no agreement linked the payment to official action.
Lack of intent — the defendant did not intend to influence official conduct.
Entrapment — law enforcement induced the defendant to offer the bribe.

prosecution_strengths: Custody records, facility logs, and officer testimony establish the defendant was in lawful custody.
The escape itself is typically documented through surveillance, roll calls, and incident reports.
Additional charges often accompany escape (assault on officers, property damage).
defense_opportunities: Duress — the defendant escaped due to imminent threats to their safety within the facility.
The custody was unlawful — if the underlying detention was without authority, escape may be justified.
The defendant was released by error and did not affirmatively escape.
Voluntary return shortly after the escape may mitigate penalties.
common_defenses: Duress — conditions in custody created a threat of serious bodily harm.
Unlawful custody — the underlying detention or arrest was without legal authority.
Administrative error — the defendant was mistakenly released and did not escape.
Voluntary return — the defendant returned to custody voluntarily.

prosecution_strengths: Veterinary evidence of the animal's condition and injuries provides expert testimony.
Photographs and video of the animal's condition are emotionally impactful evidence.
Vermont has strong animal welfare laws and public sympathy for animal cruelty cases is high.
defense_opportunities: The defendant provided reasonable care given their resources and knowledge.
The animal's condition was caused by illness or injury, not neglect or cruelty.
Agricultural or husbandry practices that are standard in the industry may not constitute cruelty.
Another person was responsible for the animal's care and caused the neglect.
common_defenses: Adequate care — the defendant provided reasonable care for the animal.
Medical condition — the animal's condition was caused by illness, not cruelty.
Agricultural exemption — the practices were standard animal husbandry.
Another caretaker was responsible for the animal.

prosecution_strengths: Probation officer testimony and supervision records document the violation.
Drug test results, missed appointments, and police reports provide objective evidence.
The original sentence can be imposed in full upon revocation.
defense_opportunities: Argue the violation was technical and minor, warranting a sanction short of revocation.
The defendant made substantial efforts to comply despite the violation.
Challenge the accuracy of the evidence (drug test false positive, incorrect reporting dates).
Present mitigating circumstances explaining the violation (job loss, homelessness, medical issues).
common_defenses: Substantial compliance — the defendant made genuine efforts to follow probation conditions.
Mitigating circumstances — external factors beyond the defendant's control caused the violation.
Challenge the evidence — false positive drug test, incorrect records.
The violation was technical and minor, not warranting revocation.

prosecution_strengths: Parole officers closely monitor parolees, generating detailed records of compliance.
GPS monitoring, drug testing, and regular check-ins provide objective evidence of violations.
The remaining sentence can be reinstated upon revocation.
defense_opportunities: Argue the violation was technical and should be addressed with graduated sanctions.
Present evidence of rehabilitation and compliance in other areas of parole conditions.
Challenge the evidence of the violation — GPS errors, testing inaccuracies.
Mitigating circumstances explain the violation without excusing it.
common_defenses: Technical violation — the violation was minor and does not warrant re-incarceration.
Rehabilitation — the parolee has made significant progress and the violation was an aberration.
Challenge the evidence — GPS tracking errors, false positive drug tests.
Mitigating circumstances — circumstances beyond the parolee's control contributed to the violation.

prosecution_strengths: Any assistance, encouragement, or facilitation of the crime can establish liability.
Electronic communications showing planning or coordination are powerful evidence.
Accomplice liability casts a wide net — the defendant need not have been physically present.
defense_opportunities: The defendant did not know a crime was being planned or committed.
Mere presence at the scene is insufficient — the defendant must have actively assisted.
The defendant withdrew from the criminal plan before the crime was committed.
The defendant's assistance was too minimal or attenuated to constitute aiding and abetting.
common_defenses: Lack of knowledge — the defendant did not know a crime was being committed.
Mere presence — the defendant was present but did not actively participate.
Withdrawal — the defendant withdrew from the plan before the crime occurred.
The defendant's alleged assistance was too minor to establish accomplice liability.

prosecution_strengths: Preparation evidence (acquiring weapons, casing a location, purchasing materials) establishes the substantial step.
Confessions or statements of intent are direct evidence of the defendant's plan.
The maximum penalty is the same as the completed offense, providing strong plea leverage.
defense_opportunities: Argue the defendant's actions were mere preparation and did not constitute a 'substantial step.'
Voluntary abandonment — the defendant chose not to complete the crime.
Legal impossibility — the crime could not have been completed under the circumstances.
The defendant's statements were aspirational or hypothetical, not indicative of genuine intent.
common_defenses: Mere preparation — the defendant's actions did not go beyond planning.
Voluntary abandonment — the defendant voluntarily stopped before completing the crime.
Impossibility — the crime could not have been completed.
Lack of intent — the defendant did not genuinely intend to commit the crime.

prosecution_strengths: Electronic communications (texts, calls, emails) documenting the agreement are powerful evidence.
Co-conspirator testimony — one participant cooperating with prosecution can establish the agreement.
Each member is liable for all acts committed in furtherance of the conspiracy.
defense_opportunities: Challenge the existence of an agreement — mere association or conversation is not conspiracy.
The defendant withdrew from the conspiracy before any overt act was committed.
The alleged co-conspirators were government agents — no genuine agreement with a private party.
The defendant's statements were hypothetical or joking, not an actual agreement to commit a crime.
common_defenses: No agreement — there was no meeting of the minds to commit a crime.
Withdrawal — the defendant withdrew from the conspiracy before completion.
Government agent — the sole co-conspirator was a government agent (no genuine conspiracy).
Lack of intent — the defendant did not intend to participate in criminal activity.
